sentences.text: In 2018 The New York Times reported that at least 90 alumni had died since the school closed, mostly of overdoses or suicide.
In 2025 a federal jury convicted Paul Geer, a longtime choir teacher there, of taking students across state lines to abuse them.
In 2026 a former student sued the family, the village of Hancock and its police for $10 million.
Tony and Betty Argiros, recovering alcoholics in a twelve-step program, began by taking young people recovering from substance abuse into their home as foster parents.

sentences.text: When the number of foster children passed New York's limit, they had the home licensed as a school.

sentences.text: Woodbury Reports dated the school's opening to 1977.
By 2000 the founders' children had taken over its day-to-day operations.
By 2011 the founders' children and grandchildren ran the school, and Mike Argiros was executive director.
Students lived in "family houses" overseen by staff called family leaders, followed a twelve-step program, and most stayed 18 months to two years or longer.

In its 2009 listing with the National Association of Therapeutic Schools and Programs, the school reported 200 students aged 12 to 18 and a minimum stay of 18 months, gave its founding year as 1979, and said it had been a member since 1999.

sentences.text: In October 2013 the school renamed itself Allynwood Academy.
On July 31, 2014, it told referral sources it would close on August 8, citing "the financial realities that we are facing."

sources.cite: Allynwood Academy letter, Woodbury Reports, July 31, 2014

sentences.text: After an outpouring of support it stayed open through the end of 2014 for 15 students and minimal staff, while about 70 employees and students were laid off or asked to leave.
In August 2014 a former student told WBNG he had been told to wake a student with a flood light, which damaged the student's eyes; a member of the Argiros family denied it.
Rita Argiros said methods such as blanket restraints and forcing students to eat all their food had since been replaced.
In September 2018 The New York Times reported on its front page that at least 90 alumni had died since the closing, mostly of overdoses or suicide.
It said the school had closed after enrollment fell in the wake of a "truth campaign" in which alumni described solitary confinement, enforced silence and restraint.
Elizabeth "Liz" Ianelli, an alumna who was there from 1995 to 1998 and led the count, took the name Survivor993 from the number of days she spent there.

sources.cite: Hachette Book Group, I See You, Survivor (2023)

sentences.text: Her tally had reached 101.
She told her story in the 2023 memoir "I See You, Survivor" and in the 2026 documentary "The Kids Are Not Alright."

sentences.text: Paul Geer taught choir at the school from 1991 until it closed and was also a family leader.

In April 2024 a federal indictment charged him with six counts involving three students: three of coercing and enticing them to travel across state lines for sexual activity, and three of transporting them across state lines for that purpose.

sources.cite: U.S. Attorney, Northern District of New York, April 4, 2024

sentences.text: He had taken them to Maine, Pennsylvania and Toronto in 1994, 2000 and 2001.
On March 3, 2025, an Albany jury convicted him on the four counts involving two of the students and could not agree on the third.
The trial evidence showed he denied students food, forced them to eat regurgitated food, bound children in rugs and isolated them.
On September 4, 2025, he was sentenced to 27 years and three months in federal prison.
Prosecutors said the punishments he imposed were "tantamount to torture".
Lawsuits followed the school's closing.
By January 2022 former students had filed at least ten lawsuits since 2019 over their time at the school, and three had been settled in October 2021.
In June 2026 a man who was a student from 2000 to 2003 sued the Argiros family, the village of Hancock and local police in federal court in Brooklyn, seeking $10 million.

His complaint, as the New York Post quoted it, said the school was run by "former alcoholics and self-identified sex addicts with no professional licensing, clinical training, or educational credentials."

It said students worked "for the direct financial benefit" of the Argiros family, "digging excavation trenches on the Argiros family estate" and "cleaning waste from the Argiros family's pig pens and farm animal enclosures."
As WION and the Post reported it, the suit also alleges students were strip-searched, locked in closets and made to dig their own graves, and that he was made to eat vomit.

It also said dogs were used to "pursue and forcibly return" students who tried to escape, and that local authorities ignored reports of abuse because of the "influence" of the owners, Michael and Cindy Argiros.
Michael Argiros has denied knowing of abuse allegations while he ran the school.
